fetched_contents.text: Protective Effects of Curcumin in Cardiovascular Diseases—Impact on Oxidative Stress and Mitochondria Abstract Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) contribute to a large part of worldwide mortality. Similarly, two of the major risk factors for these diseases, aging and obesity, are also global problems. Aging, the gradual decline of body functions, is non-modifiable. Obesity, a modifiable risk factor for CVDs, also predisposes to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Moreover, it affects not only the vasculature and the heart but also specific fat depots, which themselves have a major impact on the development and progression of CVDs. Common denominators of aging, obesity, and T2DM include oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic abnormalities such as altered lipid profiles and glucose metabolism, and inflammation. Several plant substances such as curcumin, the major active compound in turmeric root, have been used for a long time in traditional medicine and for the treatment of CVDs. Newer mechanistic, animal, and human studies provide evidence that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and attenuates numerous parameters which contribute to an increased risk for CVDs in aging as well as in obesity. Thus, curcumin as a nutraceutical could hold promise in the prevention of CVDs, but more standardized clinical trials are required to fully unravel its potential. Keywords: aging, atherosclerosis, cardiovascular diseases, curcumin, mitochondria, myocardial infarction, obesity, oxidative stress, risk factors 1. Introduction 1.1. Cardiovascular Diseases Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death worldwide. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the almost 18 million deaths due to CVDs accounted for 32% of global deaths in 2019. This report also revealed that CVDs do not exclusively affect industrialized countries, as over three-quarters of CVD-related deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/cardiovascular-diseases-(cvds) (accessed on 8 January 2022)). Older projections have already indicated that this number is expected to increase to over 23 million by 2030 [1]. In addition to being the major cause of death worldwide, CVDs also lead to a great number of chronically ill patients, and as a consequence, to an immense socio-economic burden. Thus, there is an urgent global need for efficient CVD prevention. There are numerous established risk factors for the development and progression of CVDs. The aging process per se is a non-modifiable risk factor, as it cannot be reversed. On the contrary, other factors such as obesity, which, according to the WHO report on global health risks, is one of the major causes of ischemic heart disease [2], are modifiable, meaning that measures can be taken to change them and thereby reduce the risk for CVDs. Many natural substances have been used in traditional medicine in many regions of the world, often for thousands of years. In this review, we will highlight the impact of curcumin on age-related cardiovascular dysfunction, adipose tissue, and obesity, as well as its protective effects in atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction. 1.2. Curcumin as Nutraceutical with Pleiotropic Actions Curcumin has been used as a spice, herbal supplement, food additive, and traditional medicine in Asia for more than 4000 years. It has been widely studied with respect to many diseases and is considered to have a huge potential medical benefit. The polyphenolic compound is the major active component extracted from the rhizomes of turmeric (Curcuma longa). First described by Vogel and Pelletier as a “yellow coloring-matter” in 1815 [3], the pure compound was obtained in 1842 [4]. It took until 1910 before the chemical structure was identified as diferuloylmethane [5] and another 8 years before it was synthesized [6]. The effects of this nutraceutical with regard to its anti-bacterial, anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidant, and anti-cancer properties have been studied in vitro and in vivo for a long time [7,8,9,10]; additionally, numerous clinical trials addressing various human diseases have been conducted [11]. 2. Cardiovascular Diseases and Risk Factors 2.1. Atherosclerosis and Myocardial Infarction There are various types of CVDs affecting the vessels and the heart. Atherosclerosis is a complex and multi-factorial disease driven by low-grade inflammation. During disease progression, a fibrous plaque is built up on the arterial wall leading to progredient narrowing of the vessel lumen. One of the key events in the initiation of atherosclerosis, besides cholesterol deposition in the vessel walls and chronic inflammatory reactions, is endothelial dysfunction, which occurs in areas of arteries prone to plaque development [12] that are characterized by disturbed blood flow and an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS are produced by various systems, including NADPH oxidases and the mitochondria, in endothelial as well as in smooth muscle cells [13]. Under homeostatic conditions, excessive ROS production is counteracted by anti-oxidative systems such as Glutathione (GSH), Superoxide dismutases (SODs), and Catalase, which are downregulated by various risk factors for CVDs. Oxidative stress in the vasculature does not only affect the vascular wall but also leads to the oxidation of lipids, which in turn play a critical role in atherosclerosis development and progression [14,15,16]. Seemingly, there is interdependence between lipids and oxidative stress in atherosclerosis. This is exemplified by increased mitochondrial ROS production in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor (Ldlr)-deficient mice [17], an established atherosclerosis model. Introduction Atherosclerosis is a chronic, immune-mediated disease in which lipid deposition and sustained vascular inflammation drive progressive plaque formation and arterial stiffening. Globally, it underlies ∼50 % of cardiovascular deaths, with ischaemic heart disease and stroke leading mortality statistics [1], [2]. It underlies atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACD), encompassing ischemic heart disease (IHD) and cerebrovascular disorders, including ischemic stroke, which rank as the second and third leading causes of death globally. IHD accounts for 49.2 % of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, while ischemic stroke contributes approximately 25 %. Between 1990 and 2019, global CVD prevalence nearly doubled from 271 million to 523 million, with CVD-related deaths rising from 12.1 million to 18.6 million [3]. The economic burden of CVD is substantial. Globally, CVD costs an estimated $863 billion annually, equivalent to $125 per person. In the United States, CVD accounts for 1–3 % of GDP, with coronary heart disease comprising half of these costs. In 2010, U.S. CVD costs totaled $503.2 billion, including $324.1 billion in direct healthcare expenditures and $179.1 billion in indirect costs, such as lost productivity. In Europe, CVD expenses reached $153.2 billion, with $87.3 billion in direct costs and $65.9 billion in indirect costs. These financial strains challenge healthcare systems and hinder national economic growth [4]. Epidemiological surveys show that hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking, and sedentary life-style account for > 70 % of global atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) burden. Elevated blood pressure alone doubles ASCVD risk and represents a critical modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic progression (Fig. 3). The rising global prevalence of atherosclerosis, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, reflects an epidemiologic transition driven by lifestyle changes and increased exposure to modifiable risk factors [5]. Modifiable risk factors - including diets high in sugar, fat, and salt; sedentary lifestyles; tobacco use; and excessive alcohol consumption - contribute to over 50 % of global all-cause mortality [6], [7]. These factors induce physiological and metabolic changes that exacerbate atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACD) through enhanced oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction [8]. Given the largely preventable nature of atherosclerosis, many nations are implementing comprehensive policies to reduce CVD burden through dietary interventions, physical activity promotion, and smoking cessation programs [9]. The arterial wall's three-layered structure - intima, media, and adventitia - provides the anatomical framework for atherosclerotic progression. The intima, composed of endothelial cells and subendothelial matrix, serves as the initial site for lipid accumulation and inflammatory cell recruitment. The media, containing smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers, contributes to vascular tone regulation and undergoes pathological remodeling during atherosclerosis. The adventitia, the outermost layer, contains fibroblasts, immune cells, and vasa vasorum that participate in the "outside-in" inflammatory response observed in advanced lesions [10]. The pathobiology of atherosclerosis involves a tightly orchestrated sequence of endothelial dysfunction, lipoprotein retention, oxidative stress–induced low-density lipoprotein (LDL) oxidation, and maladaptive immune activation (Fig. 1) [11]. The complex pathophysiology involves oxidative stress, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, which damage vascular endothelial cells, allowing low-density lipoproteins (LDL) to penetrate the sub-endothelial space. This triggers a cascade of events, including oxidized LDL (ox-LDL) formation, macrophage activation, and foam cell development, culminating in atherosclerotic plaque formation [12]. These plaques, composed of cholesterol, inflammatory cells, and cellular debris, underlie over 50 % of annual deaths in the U.S. due to cardiovascular events like myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke [13]. Immune dysfunction and oxidative stress further drive atherosclerosis. A Th1-mediated immune response releases interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), recruiting macrophages and smooth muscle cells while inhibiting collagen synthesis, destabilizing plaques. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), which oxidize LDL into ox-LDL, promoting endothelial damage, inflammatory cytokine release, and cell adhesion molecule expression. Additionally, ox-LDL within the intima activates macrophages into foam cells and stimulates vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation, forming atherosclerotic plaques (Fig. 1) [14], [15], [16], [17]. Atherosclerosis pathogenesis involves complex interactions between multiple cellular and molecular components. MicroRNA-33 (miR-33) plays a crucial regulatory role in cholesterol metabolism and homeostasis by targeting key genes involved in cellular cholesterol efflux, particularly ATP-binding cassette transporters ABCA1 and ABCG112. These transporters facilitate cholesterol transfer from macrophages to high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and their inhibition by miR-33 promotes foam cell formation and atherosclerotic plaque development. Understanding miR-33's function provides important context for potential therapeutic interventions targeting cholesterol metabolism (Fig. 2) [18]. Submission received: 4 February 2024 / Revised: 2 March 2024 / Accepted: 5 March 2024 / Published: 8 March 2024 Abstract Curcumin, a natural polyphenolic component from Curcuma longa roots, is the main bioactive component of turmeric spice and has gained increasing interest due to its proposed anti-cancer, anti-obesity, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and lipid-lowering effects, in addition to its thermogenic capacity. As the main bioactive component of turmeric, curcumin is a polyphenol that is relatively unstable in aqueous solution, has low bioavailability to the organs of the human body, and, upon uptake, is rapidly converted to a number of bioactive metabolites. Mechanistic explanation of how curcumin may reduce heart failure risk

Curcumin’s potential to reduce heart failure risk is best understood as a combination of antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic/anti-remodeling effects that operate at multiple levels of cardiac biology. The evidence across the provided sources consistently points to curcumin targeting oxidative stress and inflammation, while also influencing cardiac cells and remodeling pathways.

First, curcumin appears to act on oxidative stress through antioxidant and signaling pathways. The search results indicate that curcumin “reduces oxidative stress” and “attenuates numerous parameters which contribute to an increased risk for CVDs,” including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolic abnormalities [N1-R2][N1-R5]. A more specific mechanism is that curcumin may reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxidation by acting as an antioxidant and/or by modulating signaling pathways [N5-R3]. The review evidence also explicitly notes that curcumin “reduces atherosclerosis by inhibiting NF-ÎºB and MAPK signaling pathways, reducing oxidative stress, modulating lipid ...” [N1-R2]. This is highly relevant because oxidative stress is a core driver of endothelial dysfunction and cardiac injury, and reducing it can blunt the progression toward heart failure.

Second, curcumin’s anti-inflammatory action is central to its cardiovascular protection. The same review source states that curcumin “reduces atherosclerosis by inhibiting NF-ÎºB and MAPK signaling pathways,” which are well-established pro-inflammatory pathways involved in atherosclerosis and vascular inflammation [N1-R2]. Another source summarizes curcumin’s broad pleiotropic effects as including anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidant, and anti-cancer properties, with evidence in vitro and in vivo [N5-R2]. This means curcumin does not simply act as a general antioxidant; it also suppresses inflammatory cascades that contribute to endothelial dysfunction and plaque progression. In the cardiovascular context, chronic inflammation is a key contributor to atherosclerosis, endothelial damage, and ultimately to the development of heart failure.

Third, curcumin affects cardiac cells and signaling molecules by targeting fibrosis, remodeling, and apoptosis. The provided evidence shows that curcumin can “significantly protect cardiomyocyte injury after ischemia and hypoxia,” inhibit myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis, and improve ventricular remodeling [N1-R3]. Another source specifically states that curcumin alleviates cardiac remodeling in CHF-cur rabbits, including myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, apoptosis, and ultrastructure changes [N2-R3]. A separate search result also says curcumin has potential as a therapeutic target in treating adverse remodeling in ischemic heart disease [N2-R1]. These findings indicate that curcumin can modulate cardiac signaling and cell fate directly, reducing the structural and functional changes that underlie heart failure progression.

A further important mechanistic layer is endothelial function and vascular health. Curcumin has been reported to improve vascular endothelial function and protect against endothelial dysfunction in animal models of cardio-metabolic disease [N3-R2]. It can also upregulate endothelial nitric oxide production in hypertension models [N3-R3], and the review evidence states that curcumin improves endothelial function with increased NO bioavailability [N5-R2]. Endothelial dysfunction is a precursor to atherosclerosis, myocardial ischemia, and heart failure, so this vascular protection likely contributes to a lower risk of cardiac events.

Taken together, the evidence supports both direct cardiac protection and indirect risk reduction. Direct protection comes from curcumin’s effects on cardiomyocytes, fibrosis, apoptosis, and remodeling [N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1]. Indirect risk reduction comes from its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions on oxidative stress, NF-ÎºB/MAPK pathways, and endothelial function [N1-R2][N5-R3][N5-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, curcumin may reduce heart failure risk by simultaneously preserving vascular integrity, limiting cardiac injury, and preventing the pathological remodeling that leads to decompensated heart failure [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2].

One limitation of the mechanistic evidence is that the sources emphasize in vitro and animal findings, and the review explicitly notes that more standardized clinical trials are required to fully unravel curcumin’s potential [N4-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not contradict the mechanistic plausibility of the pathways; it simply highlights that translation to human heart failure outcomes remains an important next step.

Evidence and context for curcumin’s effect on heart failure outcomes

The evidence base for curcumin’s effect on heart failure outcomes is mixed in scope and strength, with stronger support for preclinical and some human studies than for definitive clinical prevention trials. Across the provided sources, the best evidence comes from animal studies, human clinical trials, and reviews that connect curcumin to cardiovascular disease endpoints rather than to heart failure itself in isolation.

In preclinical studies, the evidence is substantial. A review states that animal studies demonstrate significant improvements in cardiac function and reductions in infarct size with curcumin administration in I/R models [N4-R2]. Another review explicitly states that newer mechanistic, animal, and human studies provide evidence that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and attenuates numerous parameters contributing to CVD risk [N4-R1]. A separate search result reports cardioprotective effects of curcumin against myocardial I/R injury, mainly through anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic mechanisms [N4-R3]. These findings suggest that curcumin can improve cardiac function and reduce injury in experimental heart disease settings, which is biologically relevant to heart failure risk reduction.

The human evidence is more limited but still suggestive. The most direct human study link in the provided materials is the randomized controlled study on high-absorption curcumin for heart disease prevention, which reported that high-absorption curcumin prevented an increase in plasma brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), a marker of heart failure [N4-R5]. This is an important outcome because BNP is used clinically to assess cardiac stress and ventricular dysfunction. However, the study described is a prevention trial rather than a heart failure treatment trial, so it does not directly evaluate whether curcumin prevents heart failure onset in high-risk patients. It does, however, indicate that curcumin may affect clinically meaningful biomarkers associated with heart failure [N4-F3].

The dose, duration, and population differences across studies are important qualifiers. The human study mentioned used “high-absorption curcumin,” which implies formulation-based bioavailability optimization rather than standard curcumin [N4-F3]. The review evidence also notes that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and that more standardized clinical trials are needed [N4-F1]. This suggests that the current evidence base is not homogeneous in terms of dosage, duration, or patient populations. The provided human study excerpt does not specify a long-duration trial, which matters because chronic exposure may be needed to observe meaningful heart failure outcomes [N4-F3]. In addition, the sources emphasize that curcumin’s effects depend on formulation, bioavailability, and metabolic handling [N5-F4]. This means that results may vary across preparations and patient groups, and that a single dose or duration may not be generalizable.

The limitations are considerable. First, the evidence is largely preclinical and not yet robustly translated to human heart failure outcomes [N4-F1]. Second, study quality varies; the human trial described here is a randomized controlled study, but the review explicitly states that more standardized trials are needed [N4-F1]. Third, the bioavailability issue is a major limitation. The review on enhancing curcumin bioavailability explains that intact curcumin levels in the body may be too low (<1 μM) to affect signaling and gene expression, while higher concentrations may be needed for disease-preventing effects [N5-F4]. This means that observed effects in cultured cells or animals may not translate easily to effective oral doses in humans unless formulations are optimized.

Translation to human heart failure outcomes is therefore only partial. The human study supports the idea that curcumin may influence biomarkers of heart failure, but it does not establish whether it prevents heart failure onset or improves outcomes in established disease [N4-R5][N4-F3]. The broader review evidence also highlights that CVD prevention and risk factor modification are important, but that more work is needed to define curcumin’s role in specific heart failure subtypes [N4-F1]. In short, the evidence base is encouraging, but it remains limited by study design, formulation variability, and the need for more direct human heart failure trials [N4-F1][N5-F4].

Interpretation of curcumin’s clinical relevance for cardiac protection

The mechanistic evidence maps reasonably well to clinically meaningful outcomes, but not fully. On one hand, curcumin’s antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects are directly relevant to the pathophysiology of heart failure: it targets oxidative stress and inflammation, protects endothelial function, and modulates signaling pathways such as NF-ÎºB and MAPK [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-R3][N5-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. It also affects cardiac cells and remodeling by reducing cardiomyocyte injury, myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, apoptosis, and adverse remodeling [N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1]. These mechanisms are biologically plausible because oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, fibrosis, and remodeling are established contributors to heart failure progression and ventricular dysfunction [N2-R2][N3-R2].

The clinical evidence, however, is less direct. The strongest human link in the provided evidence is that high-absorption curcumin prevented an increase in plasma BNP, a biomarker of heart failure, in a randomized controlled study [N4-R5][N4-F3]. This suggests curcumin may influence biomarkers associated with cardiac stress, but it does not prove prevention of heart failure onset or improved outcomes in established disease. Preclinical studies show improvements in cardiac function and reductions in infarct size in I/R models and other animal studies [N4-R2][N4-R3], but these are still experimental rather than human heart failure trials [N4-F1]. So, the mechanistic evidence supports a biological rationale, while the outcome evidence supports some biomarker and animal cardiac benefits, but not yet a robust human prevention or treatment claim.

What remains uncertain is whether curcumin’s effects are durable, dose-dependent, and translatable across populations. The evidence emphasizes that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and that more standardized clinical trials are needed to fully unravel its potential [N4-F1]. The bioavailability issue is especially important: intact curcumin levels in the body may be too low (<1 μM) to affect signaling and gene expression, and higher concentrations may be needed for disease-preventing effects [N5-F4]. This means that observed effects in cultured cells or animals may not translate easily to effective oral doses in humans unless formulations are optimized. The human study cited here used “high-absorption curcumin,” which implies formulation variation rather than a universally applicable dose [N4-F3]. The provided evidence also notes that study quality varies and that more standardized trials are needed [N4-F1][N5-F4].

Practically, curcumin appears more plausible as a preventive or adjunctive strategy than as a first-line treatment for established heart failure. Its effects are likely to be more relevant to risk reduction, vascular protection, and slowing disease progression than to reversing severe heart failure [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N3-R3]. However, prevention versus treatment implies different expectations: prevention may involve long-term use of optimized formulations to reduce biomarkers and risk factors, whereas treatment would require evidence that curcumin improves outcomes in patients already diagnosed with heart failure [N4-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4]. Given the current evidence, curcumin’s clinical relevance is encouraging but still limited; it is a promising candidate for cardiovascular disease prevention, but its role in heart failure as a specific therapy remains uncertain and requires more direct human trials [N4-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence across the branch reports indicates that curcumin targets oxidative stress and inflammation, affects cardiac cells and signaling molecules, and may also improve vascular health. However, the evidence base is stronger mechanistically than clinically, and the translation to human heart failure outcomes remains limited.

### 1) Curcumin’s mechanistic pathways: antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects

These findings indicate that curcumin can modulate the signaling and cellular responses that drive heart failure progression, including fibrosis, apoptosis, and structural remodeling.

A particularly important mechanistic layer is the effect on cardiac fibrosis and remodeling. The evidence shows that cardiac fibrosis can initiate further pathological changes that ultimately can lead to heart failure, and heart failure is characterized by interstitial fibrosis [N2-R2]. Curcumin’s ability to inhibit myocardial fibrosis and improve ventricular remodeling therefore directly addresses one of the key pathophysiological features of heart failure [N1-R3][N2-R3]. ### 4) Whether evidence supports direct protection or indirect risk reduction

The evidence supports both direct cardiac protection and indirect risk reduction. Direct protection comes from curcumin’s effects on cardiomyocytes, fibrosis, apoptosis, and remodeling [N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1]. Indirect risk reduction comes from its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions on oxidative stress, NF-ÎºB/MAPK pathways, and endothelial function [N1-R2][N5-R3][N5-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In other words, curcumin may reduce heart failure risk by preserving vascular integrity, limiting cardiac injury, and preventing the pathological remodeling that leads to decompensated heart failure [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2].

### 5) Evidence for heart failure outcomes

The evidence base for curcumin’s effect on heart failure outcomes is mixed in scope and strength. The branch reports describe stronger support for preclinical and some human studies than for definitive clinical prevention trials. Preclinical studies show that animal studies demonstrate significant improvements in cardiac function and reductions in infarct size with curcumin administration in I/R models [N4-R2]. It does, however, indicate that curcumin may affect clinically meaningful biomarkers associated with heart failure [N4-F3].

### 6) Dose, duration, and population differences

The branch reports highlight important differences in study design and population. The human study cited used “high-absorption curcumin,” which implies formulation-based bioavailability optimization rather than standard curcumin [N4-F3]. The review evidence also notes that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and that more standardized clinical trials are needed [N4-F1]. ### 7) Limitations and translation issues

The main limitations are study quality and translation to humans. The evidence is largely preclinical and not yet robustly translated to human heart failure outcomes [N4-F1]. The branch reports also emphasize that more standardized clinical trials are needed to fully unravel curcumin’s potential [N4-F1]. Bioavailability is a major limitation: intact curcumin levels in the body may be too low (<1 μM) to affect signaling and gene expression, and higher concentrations may be needed for disease-preventing effects [N5-F4]. From a practical perspective, curcumin appears more plausible as a preventive or adjunctive strategy than as a first-line treatment for established heart failure. Its effects are likely to be more relevant to risk reduction, vascular protection, and slowing disease progression than to reversing severe heart failure [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N3-R3]. Prevention may involve long-term use of optimized formulations to reduce biomarkers and risk factors, whereas treatment would require evidence that curcumin improves outcomes in patients already diagnosed with heart failure [N4-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4].

### 9) Bottom line

Overall, the mechanistic evidence is strong: curcumin reduces oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and cardiac remodeling; it protects cardiomyocytes and limits fibrosis and apoptosis; and it improves vascular health through endothelial nitric oxide pathways [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-R3][N5-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1]. The clinical evidence, however, is more limited and mostly suggestive rather than definitive. The best available evidence supports curcumin as a promising candidate for cardiovascular disease prevention and for reducing biomarkers of heart failure, but it does not yet provide strong proof that curcumin prevents heart failure onset or reliably improves outcomes in established disease [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5][N4-F1][N5-F4].

The branch reports highlight important differences in study design and population. The human study cited used “high-absorption curcumin,” which implies formulation-based bioavailability optimization rather than standard curcumin [N4-F3]. The review evidence also notes that curcumin has pleiotropic effects and that more standardized clinical trials are needed [N4-F1]. This suggests that the current evidence base is not homogeneous in terms of dosage, duration, or patient populations. The provided human study excerpt does not specify a long-duration trial, which matters because chronic exposure may be needed to observe meaningful heart failure outcomes [N4-F3].

### 7) Limitations and translation issues

The main limitations are study quality and translation to humans. The evidence is largely preclinical and not yet robustly translated to human heart failure outcomes [N4-F1]. The branch reports also emphasize that more standardized clinical trials are needed to fully unravel curcumin’s potential [N4-F1]. Bioavailability is a major limitation: intact curcumin levels in the body may be too low (<1 μM) to affect signaling and gene expression, and higher concentrations may be needed for disease-preventing effects [N5-F4]. This means that observed effects in cultured cells or animals may not translate easily to effective oral doses in humans unless formulations are optimized.

Translation to human heart failure outcomes is therefore only partial. The human study supports the idea that curcumin may influence biomarkers of heart failure, but it does not establish whether it prevents heart failure onset or improves outcomes in established disease [N4-R5][N4-F3]. The broader review evidence also highlights that CVD prevention and risk factor modification are important, but that more work is needed to define curcumin’s role in specific heart failure subtypes [N4-F1]. In short, the evidence base is encouraging, but it remains limited by study design, formulation variability, and the need for more direct human heart failure trials [N4-F1][N5-F4].

### 8) Practical implications: prevention versus treatment

From a practical perspective, curcumin appears more plausible as a preventive or adjunctive strategy than as a first-line treatment for established heart failure. Its effects are likely to be more relevant to risk reduction, vascular protection, and slowing disease progression than to reversing severe heart failure [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R1][N3-R3]. Prevention may involve long-term use of optimized formulations to reduce biomarkers and risk factors, whereas treatment would require evidence that curcumin improves outcomes in patients already diagnosed with heart failure [N4-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4].

### 9) Bottom line

Overall, the mechanistic evidence is strong: curcumin reduces oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and cardiac remodeling; it protects cardiomyocytes and limits fibrosis and apoptosis; and it improves vascular health through endothelial nitric oxide pathways [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-R3][N5-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1]. The clinical evidence, however, is more limited and mostly suggestive rather than definitive. The best available evidence supports curcumin as a promising candidate for cardiovascular disease prevention and for reducing biomarkers of heart failure, but it does not yet provide strong proof that curcumin prevents heart failure onset or reliably improves outcomes in established disease [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5][N4-F1][N5-F4].

In other words, curcumin may contribute to reducing heart failure risk by protecting the heart and vasculature through multiple interconnected mechanisms, but its clinical relevance remains conditional on better human trials, optimized formulations, and longer-term study designs [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-R3][N5-R2][N1-R3][N2-R3][N2-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F1][N5-F4].
